hook.support: Everyone has a story only they can tell. A first day. A night the power went out. A lost dog. You don't need a big life. You need one moment, told well.
hook.core: Everyone has a story nobody else could tell: the night the power went out, a first shift, the day a dog went missing, the moment you realised something had changed. You don't need a dramatic life. You need one moment, told well.

why.support: True stories help people connect. They are in songs, podcasts and job interviews. Good stories have a shape. Learn it, and any moment can be worth telling.
why.core: True stories are how people connect. They're in speeches, job interviews, songs, podcasts and the ABC's Heywire competition. A good story has a shape and a few simple tools, and once you know them, you can make any moment worth listening to.
why.extend: Personal narrative sits behind job interviews, speeches, applications, songs and podcasts. Its power comes from craft: a clear shape, precise detail and a voice that sounds like you. Learning that craft turns ordinary experience into writing other people want to read.

articles.title: How a true story works

body.support:
A good true story is about **one moment**. It has four parts.

1. **Hook.** Start in the middle of the moment. *The power went out in the middle of dinner.*
2. **Build.** Say what happened. Use **details**. Use your **senses**: see, hear, smell, feel.
3. **Turn.** The moment it changed.
4. **Land.** Say what it meant to you. Keep it short.

**Grow the noun.** *A car* is plain. *My uncle's old white ute* is better.

**Show, don't tell.** Don't say *I was nervous*. Say *my hands were shaking*.

Then **edit**. Read it out loud. Cut a boring bit. Add a detail.
body.core:
A good true story isn't about your whole life. It's about **one moment**. Most good stories have four parts.

1. **Hook.** Start in the middle of the moment, not at the start of the day. *The power went out halfway through my brother's birthday dinner.* is stronger than *On Saturday I woke up at 8.*
2. **Build.** Tell what happened, with **details** and the **senses**: what you saw, heard, smelled, felt. One line of **dialogue** can show a whole person.
3. **Turn.** The moment something changed: a surprise, a choice, a mistake, a realisation.
4. **Land.** End with what it meant to you, in a line or two. Trust the reader. You don't need to explain everything.

Two tools make any story stronger.

**Grow the noun.** Add words to a noun to make it exact. *A car* tells the reader nothing. *My uncle's rusty white ute with one headlight* tells them a lot.

**Show, don't tell.** Instead of naming a feeling, show what it looked like. *I was nervous* becomes *my hands wouldn't stop shaking.*

Then **edit**. Read your story out loud. Cut the boring bits. Add one detail. Move a sentence if it works better somewhere else. Even professional writers do this many times.
body.extend:
Personal narrative works when it's focused: not a life, but **one moment** seen clearly. Most strong stories follow a four-part shape.

1. **Hook.** Open *in medias res*, in the middle of the action. *The power went out halfway through my brother's birthday dinner* drops the reader straight in; *On Saturday I woke up at 8* makes them wait.
2. **Build.** Develop the moment with precise **detail**, sensory language and, where it helps, a line of **dialogue**, which can reveal a character faster than description.
3. **Turn.** The point of change: a surprise, a decision, a mistake, a realisation. It's what makes a recount a story.
4. **Land.** Close with reflection, briefly. A resonant final line usually beats a summary.

Two language tools add power. **Expanded noun groups** make description exact: *my uncle's rusty white ute with one headlight*. **Showing rather than telling** lets readers infer feelings from actions and images: *my hands wouldn't stop shaking*. Sentence patterns shape **tone** too: short sentences build tension; longer ones slow things down.

Finally, **edit** in layers: read aloud, remove repetition, refine word choices, reorder for impact.

caseStudies.title: Real stories, real audience

body.support:
Every year, the ABC runs a competition called **Heywire**. It's for young people aged **16 to 22** who live in the country.

You send in a **true story** about your life. You can write it. Or you can make a video, a recording or photos.

Winners work with the ABC to share their story across Australia. They also win a trip to **Canberra**.

Your story can be about anything. Work. Sport. Family. Your town. It works when it is **honest** and full of **real detail**.
body.core:
Every year, the ABC runs a competition called **Heywire**. It's for young people aged **16 to 22** who live in **regional, rural or remote** Australia.

The rules are simple. Send in a **true story** about your life and the place where you live. You can write it, or tell it with **audio, video or photos**. You don't need to be a writer.

Each ABC regional station picks a winner for its area. Winners work with ABC producers to share their story around the country. They also win a free trip to Canberra for the **Heywire Regional Youth Summit**. There, they meet other winners and share ideas for their communities.

Your story can be about anything in your life: work, sport, family, your town, or a hard time and how you got through it. It doesn't need to be dramatic. It needs to be **one moment, told honestly, with real detail**.
body.extend:
Each year, the ABC's **Heywire** competition invites young people aged **16 to 22** from **regional, rural and remote** Australia to share a **true story**. It can be about their life and the place they live. Entries can be written, or told through audio, video or photos.

Every ABC regional station selects a winner. Winners work with ABC producers to develop their stories and share them nationally. They also attend the **Heywire Regional Youth Summit** in Canberra, where they work on ideas for issues facing young people in their communities.

Heywire is a useful model for personal narrative. It asks for exactly what good stories need: a specific moment, an honest voice and precise detail. A story doesn't have to be extraordinary to work. It has to be told well.

model.text:
**Hook:** The first time I drove the ute, I put it straight through Dad's fence.

**Build:** I was twelve. Dad said I could move it ten metres, from the shed to the gate. Ten metres. How hard could it be?

**Turn:** I pushed the pedal. The ute jumped like a kicked dog. I grabbed the wheel, shut my eyes and heard wood snap. When I opened them, Dad was standing in the gap where the fence used to be.

**Land:** He looked at the fence. He looked at me. “Well,” he said. “Now you know where the brake isn't.”

teacher.overview: Students write a personal narrative about one moment from their own lives, using a four-part shape (hook, build, turn, land), expanded noun groups, sensory detail and showing rather than telling, then edit it by cutting, adding and moving. The case study is the ABC's Heywire competition, which gives regional students aged 16–22 a real audience for true stories.
prep: Write your own short true story (or use the made-up model) to model with. Students engage far more when you go first.
Check the ABC Heywire site for current competition dates if your students are regional and 16 or older.
Decide where finished stories go: a class anthology, a display, a recording, or Heywire.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — The shape
steps: **Hook (10 min):** tell (don't read) a short true story of your own. Ask: where did it start? Where did it change?
**Explicit teaching (10 min):** hook, build, turn, land, using the model story.
**Read (15 min):** article and Check your reading.
**Annotate (10 min):** Anatomy of a true story.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — The tools
steps: **Explicit teaching (10 min):** grow the noun; show, don't tell. Model live on the board.
**Tables (20 min):** Grow the noun; Show, don't tell.
**Find your story (15 min):** brainstorm, choose one moment.
**Case study (5 min):** real stories, real audience.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Write
steps: **Write (35 min):** final mission. Conference with students as they write.
**Exit (5 min):** read your hook to a partner.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Edit
steps: **Model (10 min):** edit a paragraph of your own story aloud: cut, add, move.
**Share, Level Up, reflect (20 min):** read-aloud volunteers; quick check; request sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**Four parts:** hook, build, turn, land. **Grow the noun:** add words to a noun to make it exact (*a car* → *my uncle's rusty white ute*). **Show happy (sample):** *I couldn't stop grinning the whole way home.*

**Model story:** 1 hook (starts in the moment); 2 grow the noun (stubby green candle); 3 senses (sound: fridge, rain); 4 dialogue (shows Dad's humour); 5 turn (the laugh; *in weeks* hints at a hard time); 6 land (what mattered, without over-explaining).

**Samples:** the car → *Mum's dusty silver hatchback with the cracked windscreen*; a room → *the tiny back room that always smelled of wet towels*; It was cold → *My breath hung in the air and my fingers went numb.*

realityCheck: **True stories can go deep.** Some students will choose painful moments. Tell everyone up front: choose a story you're happy for your teacher to read, and you never have to share it with the class. If a story raises a safety concern, follow your school's child-safety and reporting obligations.
**“Nothing's ever happened to me.”** You'll hear this. Small moments work best: a first shift, a lost phone, a meal, a long drive. Model with a small story of your own.
**Writing volume is a barrier.** Let students draft by voice (recording, speech-to-text) and edit the transcript. The craft is the same.
**Real audience lifts quality.** A class anthology, a display or a Heywire entry (for regional students aged 16–22) changes how hard students try.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's low-tech and personal, and many students produce their best writing of the year when it's about their own lives.
